text.p: Britain's opposition Labour Party said on Monday that it would veto any extension of majority voting in the European Union's social chapter on workers' rights.
Finance spokesman Gordon Brown said Labour was committed to signing up to the social chapter, but would adopt "a balanced and moderate approach" to its implementation.

"It is absolutely right to sign the social chapter," Brown said in an interview on BBC radio, several hours before he was due to address the Confederation of British Industry (CBI) annual conference in Harrogate.
"It is wrong for people to say that a Labour government would remove the requirement of unanimity for changes in social security or for changes in co-determination in the boardroom."
"I'm going to make it absolutely clear today, as has always been clear to the Labour Party, we will veto any attempt to do that," Brown said.
The European Union takes most of its important decisions by a consensus of all 15 members.
Any move towards extending the areas in which majority-voting is the norm is seen by Britain's vociferous "Euro-sceptics" as an unacceptable erosion of national sovereignty.

British business leaders are divided about closer European integration, with some welcoming the possible benefits of a single European currency while others are worried that the social chapter would increase their costs.
Conservative government ministers criticised Brown's comments, saying the social chapter would destroy jobs in Britain.

Defence secretary Michael Portillo, who is also attending the CBI conference, said the social chapter was "a catalogue of job-destroying measures" and signing up it was itself a massive extension of majority voting.
"The vast majority of the important aspects of the social chapter are settled by qualified majority voting," Portillo said.
Trade minister Ian Lang accused Labour of trying to perpetrate a "disgraceful con-trick" by arguing that Britain could choose which aspects of the social chapter to accept.
"The only way we can preserve Britain's veto on job destroying social costs is by keeping (Prime Minister) John Major's opt-out of the social chapter and not signing it," he said.
Deputy Prime Minister Michael Heseltine said signing the chapter would destroy Britain's competitiveness.
He told the BBC that the presence of 1,600 German companies and 1,300 French companies in Britain proved these businesses viewed the British economy more favourably than their own.
"Their own is characterised by the sort of social contract, social costs that Gordon Brown confirmed this morning that he intends to impose on the British employing groups," he said.
